query: For high-entropy alloys intended for aerospace fasteners, what single intervention could improve the combination of mechanical durability, room-temperature creep resistance, and corrosion resistance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence that supports it, and an experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Adding an optimized amount of aluminum (around 0.7 mol ratio) to a baseline CoCrFeNi‐based high-entropy alloy for aerospace fasteners will transform part of its FCC microstructure into a more BCC‐dominated structure, leading to enhanced solid-solution strengthening, reduced room-temperature creep (via lower strain rate sensitivity), and improved formation of a protective oxide layer that boosts corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: A CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy with a primarily FCC structure used in aerospace fasteners.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled doping of aluminum at approximately 0.7 mol fraction into the alloy’s composition.
generation.conditions: Tests at room temperature under mechanical load (e.g., static tensile and nanoindentation creep tests) and in corrosive environments (e.g., 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution or equivalent sulfuric acid environments) representative of aerospace service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A phase transformation and lattice distortion induced by Al addition that partially converts the FCC matrix into a BCC (or mixed) structure with finer grain sizes and a more uniform distribution of elements.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum’s large atomic radius induces lattice distortions that increase solid-solution strengthening and promote the formation of a thermodynamically stable BCC phase. This phase change decreases creep strain rates at room temperature and facilitates the development of a denser, more stable oxide/passivation film, thus enhancing corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated alloy, the Al-doped alloy is expected to exhibit a measurable increase in yield strength (e.g., an improvement on the order of 10–20%), a lower room-temperature creep rate (evidenced by a reduced strain rate sensitivity m), and a reduced corrosion current density (indicating improved corrosion resistance).
generation.baseline: The untreated CoCrFeNi-based HEA with predominantly FCC structure, whose mechanical durability, room-temperature creep behavior, and corrosion resistance represent current performance levels for aerospace fasteners.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected when the aluminum addition is optimized (around 0.7 mol ratio) and maintained below levels that might excessively reduce ductility. The beneficial effect is presumed to hold under typical aerospace service conditions at room temperature and in moderately corrosive environments. Extreme conditions or excessive Al could lead to trade-offs not accounted for here.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in yield strength, creep resistance, and corrosion performance is not precisely known and may depend on other alloying components and processing conditions. There is also some uncertainty regarding potential trade-offs in ductility and toughness with increased Al content.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set with the baseline CoCrFeNi composition and one set with the same alloy doped with approximately 0.7 mol fraction Al. Process both sets under identical thermomechanical treatment conditions. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests, nanoindentation creep tests, and electrochemical corrosion tests (potentiodynamic polarization in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution).
measurements: Yield strength and ductility from tensile tests
Creep strain rate and strain rate sensitivity (m) from nanoindentation creep tests
Corrosion current density (Icorr) and passivation behavior from potentiodynamic polarization curves
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-doped alloy does not exhibit statistically significant improvements—specifically, at least a 10–20% increase in yield strength, a lower creep strain rate (or m value reduced by a comparable percentage), and a measurable decrease (e.g., at least 20%) in corrosion current density—compared to the baseline alloy, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In the present investigation, Ti-V-Nb-Ta samples were subjected to thermal aging for various durations at 700°C. The microstructure and mechanical properties of Ti-V-Nb-Ta before and after thermal aging were revealed by a combination of state-of-the-art microstructural characterization and nanoindentation techniques. Results indicate that impurity interstitials at the trace levels within the solid solution encourage the formation of α-Ti precipitates in the Ti-V-Nb-Ta alloy when aged at high temperature, which undermines the effects of interstitial solid solution strengthening and leads to softening.

Structural components used in high-temperature environments often fail due to high-temperature creep. Traditional creep tests, such as uniaxial tensile or compression tests, often require large sample sizes and long testing periods, which has limited the research on the creep properties of RHEAs. To overcome these limitations, the use of nanoindentation techniques for studying creep behavior offers an effective alternative. Nanoindentation is applying a small indentation load on the surface of the material to measure its mechanical properties, allowing for the assessment of creep properties at a very small scale. The advantages of this technique include the small size of samples required and short experimental periods. Existing research indicates that adding Al to CoCrFeNiCu alloys results in a phase transformation from FCC to BCC structures. Although this addition reduces the ductility of the alloy, it effectively enhances its creep resistance at the nanoscale [].
